analysis.one_liner: Requires drugmakers to pay Medicaid-style rebates on drugs dispensed to low-income Medicare enrollees.
analysis.headline: The Medicare Drug Savings Act died in the Senate Finance Committee without a hearing or vote after being referred there on February 1, 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required prescription drug manufacturers to pay the government a rebate, modeled on the Medicaid rebate formula, for each drug dispensed to low-income Medicare enrollees — people who qualify for the Part D low-income subsidy or for Medicaid. A manufacturer that refused to sign a rebate agreement would have lost coverage for its drugs under Medicare's drug benefit. Medicare drug plans would have had to report dispensing and pricing data to make the rebates workable, with fines for late or false reports, and the money collected would be deposited into Medicare's drug account.
analysis.who_benefits: Low-income Medicare enrollees — seniors and disabled beneficiaries who also qualify for Medicaid or the Part D low-income subsidy — and Medicare's finances generally. The rebates would flow into Medicare's drug account, lowering the program's cost of covering this population, which ultimately eases pressure on premiums and on taxpayers.

how_it_helps.text: Requires drug manufacturers to pay a rebate for each drug dispensed to 'rebate eligible individuals' — Medicare enrollees who receive the Part D low-income subsidy or are eligible for Medicaid [S2][S3].
The rebate equals the amount by which the Medicaid rebate formula exceeds what Medicare drug plans already negotiated from the manufacturer for that drug [S3].
Manufacturers that decline to sign a rebate agreement would lose coverage of their drugs under the Medicare Part D benefit, giving them a strong financial reason to participate [S3].

Medicare drug plans and Medicare Advantage plans must report dispensing, pricing, and discount data to manufacturers and the government, with civil penalties of $10,000 per day for late data and up to $100,000 per false item [S2][S3].
All rebate money is deposited into Medicare's prescription drug account, so the savings stay inside the Medicare program rather than going to general revenue [S3].
The bill excludes these new Medicare rebates from the Medicaid 'best price' and average manufacturer price calculations, so the Medicare discounts would not reduce rebates owed to Medicaid [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers, which would owe the government a rebate on every prescription dispensed to roughly the millions of Medicare enrollees who also qualify for Medicaid or the low-income subsidy. Medicare drug plans would bear new reporting and compliance costs.

drawbacks.text: The savings go to Medicare's account, not directly into patients' pockets — a low-income enrollee's copays would not automatically fall; the benefit is program-level savings that shows up indirectly in premiums and program costs [S3].
The rebate only covers low-income enrollees, so it leaves Medicare's drug prices for everyone else untouched and does not address the broader cost of Part D [S3].

Drugmakers have long argued that government-set rebate formulas like Medicaid's shrink the revenue that funds research into new medicines, and plan sponsors would face real administrative burden and penalty exposure; the bill's designers tried to blunt the price-spillover risk by carving the new rebates out of Medicaid's 'best price' rule [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The savings would come from a targeted population — low-income Medicare enrollees who are already the cheapest group for manufacturers to serve at the Medicaid-negotiated rate — so the design is a moderate, incremental step rather than a structural overhaul of drug pricing. The main cost falls on a single, highly profitable industry, and the administrative lift for plans is real but modest. The honest limitation is that it would not lower prices for the majority of Medicare beneficiaries who are not low-income.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced and sat there without a hearing, markup, or floor vote until the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Senator Bill Nelson of Florida introduced the bill on February 1, 2017, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the same day [S5].
Fifteen senators cosponsored the bill — 13 Democrats and 2 independents; no Republican did [S4].
The Senate Finance Committee took no further action, and the bill received no vote in either chamber before the Congress ended on January 3, 2019 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers, which avoided a new rebate obligation on every prescription dispensed to low-income Medicare enrollees. Medicare and taxpayers did not receive the savings the bill would have produced.

sides.party_line_note: Every cosponsor was a Democrat or independent, and the bill died in the Republican-run Finance Committee without ever reaching the floor.

industries.note: They would owe Medicaid-style rebates on drugs dispensed to low-income Medicare enrollees, and a refusal to pay would cost them Part D coverage. The industry's gain from the bill dying was the savings Medicare did not receive.

industries.industry: Medicare Part D and Medicare Advantage drug plans
industries.note: Plans would face new data-reporting duties and penalties of $10,000 per day for late reports, but their core revenue under the program would not change.
